title: Fault Finding: An Open Branch
description: The same circuit as Series-Parallel 1 (12 V, R1 = 100 Ω in series with R2 ∥ R3 = 200 Ω each), but R3 has failed open. Healthy, the circuit draws 60 mA with 6 V across the group. Measure the faulted circuit and identify the readings that give the open away.

tasks.question: With R3 open, what total current does the source supply?
With R3 open, what is the voltage across R2?
What current flows through the open R3?
With R3 open, what is the voltage across R1? (Healthy it was 6 V.)
Which measurement most clearly indicates that R3 is open?
choices: R3 has the full parallel-group voltage across it but carries zero current
R3 has zero volts across it
The total current is higher than in the healthy circuit
The voltage across R1 is higher than in the healthy circuit

tasks.question: Compared with the healthy circuit (60 mA total, 6 V across the group), how did the open change the circuit?
choices: Total current rose and the group voltage fell
Total current fell and the group voltage rose
Nothing changed because the other branch still works
The source voltage dropped to zero

hints: An open has infinite resistance. Remove R3 from the drawing: the circuit is now just R1 (100 Ω) in series with R2 (200 Ω).
R_total rises from 200 Ω to 300 Ω, so the total current falls. V_R1 falls with it, and by KVL the group voltage rises.

An open branch still has voltage across it (the same 8 V as the rest of the group) but no current. An open element in a parallel group does not show source voltage, unlike an open in a pure series loop.
In the field: a branch that reads normal voltage but zero current (clamp meter) is open somewhere in that branch.
learningGoals: Predict how an open branch changes total resistance, total current and the voltage distribution.
Distinguish the signature of an open in a parallel branch from an open in a series path.
Use voltage and current measurements together to localize a fault.
disclaimer: Simulated bench exercise; not field experience.
